subChunks.title: Range, List, and Hash Partitioning
subChunks.hookHtml: When a single table grows to hundreds of gigabytes, partitioning splits it into smaller physical tables while presenting a unified logical interface. The right partitioning strategy can reduce query time from minutes to seconds.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Declarative partitioning (PostgreSQL 10+)

-- Parent table (partitioned):
CREATE TABLE events (
  id         BIGSERIAL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  payload    JSONB
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

-- Child partitions:
CREATE TABLE events_2024_01
  PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');

CREATE TABLE events_2024_02
  PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01');

Partition types

  • RANGE — partition by value ranges (dates, IDs). Best for time-series data.
  • LIST — partition by explicit value lists (regions, status types).
  • HASH — partition by hash of a column value. Even distribution; no natural query affinity.

Partition pruning

When a query includes WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31', the planner queries only the January 2024 partition — all other partitions are skipped. This is partition pruning.

-- Creates and queries only the relevant partition:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-02-01';
-- Plan shows: Append > Seq Scan on events_2024_01 (only 1 partition)

Partition management

-- Drop old data instantly (no row-by-row DELETE):
DROP TABLE events_2022_01;  -- instant — drops the whole partition

-- Detach a partition for archiving:
ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2022_01;

Partitioning trade-offs

  • ✅ Partition pruning dramatically speeds range queries on the partition key
  • ✅ Old data can be dropped by dropping a partition (instant vs slow DELETE)
  • ❌ Cross-partition queries (JOINs, queries without the partition key) touch all partitions
  • ❌ Unique constraints must include the partition key
  • ❌ Added complexity in schema management

storyBeats.text: The events table has 50 billion rows. Deleting last year's data takes 8 hours. A query for 'today only' scans everything.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Partition by time when you query by time. Partition pruning means a query for January only touches January's partition — the other eleven months are invisible to it. And dropping last year is instant — you are dropping a partition, not deleting fifty billion rows one at a time.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Partitioning design

Design a partitioned schema for an audit_logs(id, user_id, event_type, created_at, payload) table with these requirements: (1) queries almost always filter by date range, (2) logs older than 1 year must be purged monthly, (3) table grows by ~50M rows/month.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Partitioning strategy: RANGE on created_at, monthly partitions.

CREATE TABLE audit_logs (
  id         BIGSERIAL,
  user_id    INTEGER NOT NULL,
  event_type TEXT    NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  payload    JSONB
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

-- Create current and upcoming partitions:
CREATE TABLE audit_logs_2024_05
  PARTITION OF audit_logs
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-05-01') TO ('2024-06-01');

-- Index on each partition (user_id is common filter):
CREATE INDEX ON audit_logs_2024_05 (user_id, created_at);

-- Monthly purge (instant):
DROP TABLE audit_logs_2023_04;  -- drops 50M rows in milliseconds

-- Automate partition creation with pg_partman extension or cron job.

-- Why range/monthly:
-- Partition pruning: WHERE created_at BETWEEN x AND y touches 1-2 partitions
-- Purge: drop a partition vs DELETE 50M rows (minutes → milliseconds)
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain why hash partitioning does not benefit from partition pruning for typical application queries, and describe a use case where hash partitioning is appropriate.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Hash partitioning distributes rows evenly across N partitions based on a hash of the key value. There is no natural range or list relationship between partition number and key value.

Why no pruning: a query WHERE user_id = 123 would need to know which partition contains user 123. Without a predicate on the partition key that maps to a specific partition, the planner must check all partitions. (PostgreSQL 11+ does support hash partition pruning for equality conditions — it computes the hash to find the right partition — but range and list conditions do not prune hash-partitioned tables.)

Use case: when even data distribution matters more than query locality. Example: a multi-tenant SaaS where each tenant has roughly equal data. Hash-partitioned on tenant_id with N=16 partitions means each partition is 1/16 of total data. This helps with maintenance parallelism and sets a natural scale-out boundary, even without query pruning benefits.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain partition pruning with a time-series example. How does the database know which partition to skip?

options: The query planner skips partitions whose range cannot contain rows matching the WHERE clause
Removing old partitions to free disk space
questions.answer: The query planner skips partitions whose range cannot contain rows matching the WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Partition pruning is the planner's ability to exclude entire partitions from query execution. A WHERE clause on the partition key that excludes certain ranges causes the planner to skip those partitions entirely.

questions.prompt: What is the fastest way to delete all data from January 2022 in a monthly-range-partitioned events table?
options: DROP TABLE events_2022_01 — drops the partition in milliseconds
DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2022-01-01' AND created_at < '2022-02-01'
ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2022_01 then DELETE FROM it
questions.answer: DROP TABLE events_2022_01 — drops the partition in milliseconds
questions.explanation: Dropping a partition drops the entire physical storage segment — no row-by-row processing. DELETE would process potentially millions of rows and generate WAL entries for each. DROP TABLE is O(1) regardless of partition size.

questions.prompt: A query `SELECT * FROM events` with no WHERE clause on a 24-partition table. How many partitions are scanned?
options: All 24 — no partition key filter means no pruning
questions.answer: All 24 — no partition key filter means no pruning
questions.explanation: Partition pruning requires a WHERE condition on the partition key that narrows the value range. Without such a condition, the planner must include all partitions. This is why partitioning helps range queries but can hurt queries that scan the entire dataset.

questions.prompt: A partitioned table has unique constraint (id). A query requires UNIQUE on (id, created_at). Why must the partition key be included?
options: PostgreSQL requires the partition key to be part of unique constraints — it cannot enforce global uniqueness across partitions without it
UNIQUE constraints do not work on partitioned tables
The partition key must be the primary key
Unique constraints are per-partition by default and need the partition key to merge across partitions
questions.answer: PostgreSQL requires the partition key to be part of unique constraints — it cannot enforce global uniqueness across partitions without it
questions.explanation: Each partition is a separate physical table. A unique index only spans one physical table. PostgreSQL cannot enforce cross-partition uniqueness without the partition key as part of the constraint — the key determines which partition a row lives in, making the index per-partition valid.
